strengths: The paper addresses a useful problem: predicting human response times under changing external stimuli. Combining learned task representations with sequential evidence accumulation is a plausible contribution to cognitive modeling.

The two-day study provides substantial repeated-trial data from 36 analyzed participants across four stimulus schedules. Randomized group assignment and repeated-measures analysis give the modeling effort an empirical foundation.

The evaluation includes feature-representation comparisons and four training protocols, including leave-one-participant-out testing. The hybrid model achieves lower aggregate MAPE than Pure DRL in every protocol, providing preliminary evidence of predictive value. Reported training times on identical hardware also suggest a computational benefit.
weaknesses: Core methodological details are missing from the supplied manuscript. Referenced Appendices S2–S6 are absent, leaving the DRL algorithm, reward, diffusion dynamics, time discretization, mapping from SVM predictions to accumulation parameters, and important training settings unspecified. Code and data availability are only promised. These omissions prevent reproduction and a sound assessment of the central model.

The comparisons do not isolate the proposed contribution. Pure DRL changes both the temporal formulation and the accumulation mechanism, so its comparison with the hybrid model is not a controlled DDM ablation. Stronger alternatives include stimulus-aware supervised regression, a matched sequential neural predictor, and a DDM with stimulus-dependent parameters. The assertion that DDM principally supports posterior estimation also understates its predictive capabilities; positioning against predictive DDM, urgency, and existing RL–DDM approaches needs greater precision.

The mechanistic interpretation exceeds the evidence. Trial-level choices and response times do not uniquely identify within-trial evidence or action trajectories. Figure 3 even shows nonzero 'time pressure effect' trajectories for the no-pressure condition, suggesting that these corrections can absorb baseline prediction error. Agreement with aggregate behavioral trends does not independently validate the proposed habituation or regulation mechanisms.

The defining claim about dynamic stimuli is insufficiently tested. The progress bar follows a fixed repeating schedule, and there are no time-only, blank-frame, or altered-stimulus ablations demonstrating that frame content contributes beyond elapsed time and trial-level information. Evaluation on independently varied within-trial stimulus schedules would directly test the claimed advantage.

The predictive gains need uncertainty estimates: Figure 3(m) reports MAPE reductions from 0.3034 to 0.2999 for general-level training and from 0.3037 to 0.2905 for LOPO. Without repeated-run results or participant-level confidence intervals for the differences, their reliability is unclear. Likewise, the 4.42 versus 38.30 minute comparison measures convergence under different reward formulations rather than time to matched predictive performance.

The evaluation pipeline is ambiguous about which no-pressure observations train the baseline SVMs and whether their fitting, normalization, and hyperparameter selection occur entirely within each training fold. Consequently, leakage-free LOPO performance cannot be verified. Shuffled trial splits also do not establish prospective temporal prediction.

The behavioral conclusions require qualification. The analyzed groups contain only 7–10 participants, and three participants were excluded as extreme outliers without a stated criterion. Only the random-versus-none response-time contrast is reported as significant, which does not establish that random stimulation is superior to every alternative. Nonsignificant accuracy differences likewise do not establish an absence of accuracy effects.
A minor numerical inconsistency should be corrected: the counts in Figure 2(g) imply 4067 correct predictions out of 4083, approximately 99.61% accuracy, whereas the text reports 99.93%.
